os-memory-management:0.prompt: Which hardware component translates the logical (virtual) addresses generated by the CPU into physical addresses at run time?
options: The disk controller
The memory management unit (MMU)
The linker
The L1 data cache
os-memory-management:0.explanation: The MMU performs translation on every memory access at run time (using relocation registers or page tables). The linker resolves symbols before execution, it does not translate addresses on each access; caches store data, not mappings (the TLB caches translations but is part of the MMU path).

os-memory-management:0.prompt: A process must be movable to a different region of physical memory while it is running (e.g., after being swapped out and back in). At which stage must address binding happen?
options: Compile time
Load time
Execution time
Link time
os-memory-management:0.explanation: Only execution-time binding (with hardware such as an MMU) lets a process move during execution, because every address is translated on each access. Load-time binding fixes physical addresses when the program is loaded, so moving it later would require reloading it.

os-memory-management:0.prompt: A system uses a relocation (base) register set to 14000. A user process generates logical address 346. Which physical address is accessed?
os-memory-management:0.explanation: With dynamic relocation, physical = relocation register + logical = 14000 + 346 = 14346. Subtracting (13654) is a common slip; the process never sees 14346, it only ever works with logical address 346.

os-memory-management:0.prompt: A process has relocation register 30000 and limit register 3000. It generates logical address 3200. What happens?
options: The MMU traps to the OS with an addressing error
Physical address 33200 is accessed
The address wraps around to logical address 200
Physical address 3200 is accessed directly
os-memory-management:0.explanation: The MMU first checks logical < limit. 3200 >= 3000, so it raises a trap (addressing error) before adding the base. Accessing 33200 would let the process read memory belonging to someone else, which is exactly what the limit check prevents.

os-memory-management:0.prompt: After fork(), parent and child both print the address of the same global variable and see the identical value, yet each sets it to a different number without affecting the other. Why?
options: The OS stores two copies at the same physical address and switches them on context switch
Pointer values are printed relative to the stack pointer, so they always match
The same virtual address maps to different physical frames in each process once a write occurs (copy-on-write)
The variable lives in a CPU register, not in memory
os-memory-management:0.explanation: Printed pointers are virtual addresses. Each process has its own page table; after fork the page is shared copy-on-write, and the first write gives the writer its own physical frame at the same virtual address. A physical address cannot hold two values, so the 'switch on context switch' idea is wrong.

os-memory-management:0.prompt: On Linux, `ps` shows a Node.js process with VSZ around 10 GB but RSS around 200 MB on a machine with 8 GB of RAM. What is the best explanation?
options: The process is leaking 10 GB and will be OOM-killed shortly
Most of the virtual address space is reserved or mapped but never touched, so it has no physical frames behind it
Linux compresses the process's memory 50:1 in RAM
VSZ counts the whole machine's memory, RSS counts only this process
os-memory-management:0.explanation: VSZ is the size of the virtual address space (heap reservations, thread stacks, mapped libraries); RSS is what is actually resident in physical frames. Virtual memory can greatly exceed RAM because frames are only allocated on first touch. A large VSZ alone does not indicate a leak; a growing RSS would.

os-memory-management:0.prompt: Why can a shared library such as libc be mapped at a different virtual address in each process (e.g., with ASLR) while its code pages are still shared in physical memory?
options: It is compiled as position-independent code, using PC-relative addressing and indirection tables instead of absolute addresses
The kernel patches every absolute address in the code each time a process loads it
Each process gets its own private copy of the library's code pages
The MMU ignores the virtual address for code pages and uses the physical one
os-memory-management:0.explanation: Position-independent code avoids absolute addresses (using PC-relative addressing plus the GOT/PLT), so the same read-only physical pages work at any virtual base. Patching code per process (load-time relocation) would dirty the pages and destroy sharing, which is why PIC is preferred.

os-memory-management:0.prompt: A program was compiled with compile-time (absolute) address binding for start address 0x4000. The OS now needs to load it at 0x8000. What is required?
options: Nothing; the MMU adds 0x4000 to every address
Recompiling (or relinking) the program for the new start address
Setting the limit register to 0x8000
Restarting the OS so memory is cleared
os-memory-management:0.explanation: With compile-time binding the generated code contains absolute physical addresses, so a different start location means generating new code. Relying on the MMU to add an offset is execution-time binding, which this program was not built for.

os-memory-management:0.prompt: Which are benefits of execution-time address binding with an MMU? Select all that apply.
options: A process can be relocated in physical memory, e.g., after swapping
Each memory access can be checked against bounds or protection bits
Different processes can use the same logical addresses without conflict
It removes the need for any address translation hardware
It guarantees there is never any external fragmentation
os-memory-management:0.explanation: Run-time translation enables relocation, protection checks and independent address spaces. It needs translation hardware rather than removing it, and contiguous allocation with base/limit relocation still suffers external fragmentation (paging is what removes it).

os-memory-management:0.prompt: With execution-time binding, a user program can compute a physical address and dereference it directly to bypass the MMU.
options: True
False
os-memory-management:0.explanation: False. Every address a user program issues is treated as logical and goes through the MMU; user code never deals in physical addresses. That isolation is the whole point of the logical/physical split.

os-memory-management:0.prompt: In compile-time and load-time binding, the logical and physical addresses of a program are the same; they only differ under execution-time binding.
options: True
False
os-memory-management:0.explanation: True. Compile- and load-time binding fix physical addresses before execution, so the CPU emits physical addresses directly. Only execution-time binding introduces a separate logical (virtual) address that the MMU maps at run time.

os-memory-management:1.prompt: A system has 32-bit virtual addresses and 4 KB pages. How many entries does a single-level page table per process need?
options: 2^32 (about 4 billion)
2^20 (about 1 million)
os-memory-management:1.explanation: 4 KB = 2^12, so 12 bits are the offset and 32 - 12 = 20 bits are the page number, giving 2^20 entries. 2^12 is the number of bytes per page, not the number of pages.

os-memory-management:1.prompt: Which kind of fragmentation does paging eliminate?
options: Internal fragmentation
Fragmentation inside the page table
Both internal and external fragmentation
External fragmentation
os-memory-management:1.explanation: Any free frame can hold any page, so there are no unusable holes between allocations (external fragmentation). Internal fragmentation remains: the last page of a process is usually only partly used.

os-memory-management:1.prompt: With 4,096-byte pages, a process needs 72,766 bytes. How much internal fragmentation does it have?
options: 962 bytes
3,134 bytes
0 bytes
4,096 bytes
os-memory-management:1.explanation: 72,766 / 4,096 = 17.76, so 18 pages (73,728 bytes) are allocated; 73,728 - 72,766 = 962 bytes are wasted. 3,134 is how much of the last page is used, not how much is wasted.

os-memory-management:1.prompt: Page size is 1,024 bytes. Logical address 2,500 is accessed, and the page table maps page 2 to frame 5. What is the physical address?
os-memory-management:1.explanation: Page = 2500 div 1024 = 2, offset = 2500 - 2048 = 452. Physical = frame * page size + offset = 5 * 1024 + 452 = 5,572. Using 1,000 instead of 1,024 gives 5,452, a classic decimal slip.

os-memory-management:1.prompt: When a page is evicted, which page table entry bit lets the OS skip writing it back to disk?
options: The valid (present) bit
The referenced (accessed) bit
The dirty (modified) bit
The execute-disable bit
os-memory-management:1.explanation: The hardware sets the dirty bit on any write to the page. If it is clear, the copy on disk (file or swap) is still current, so the frame can be reused without I/O. The referenced bit tracks recent use for replacement decisions, not modification.

os-memory-management:1.prompt: x86-64 uses 48-bit virtual addresses, 4 KB pages and 8-byte page table entries. Roughly how large would a flat single-level page table be per process?
options: 512 GB
4 MB
256 TB
32 MB
os-memory-management:1.explanation: 48 - 12 = 36 bits of page number, so 2^36 entries * 8 bytes = 2^39 bytes = 512 GB per process, which is why multi-level tables are used. 256 TB is the size of the whole 48-bit address space, not of the table.

os-memory-management:1.prompt: Redis runs BGSAVE (fork, then the child writes a snapshot). Under a write-heavy load, total memory use rises sharply during the save, and it is worse with transparent huge pages enabled. Why?
options: The child copies the entire dataset into its own memory before writing it out
Copy-on-write duplicates every page the parent writes to during the snapshot, and with 2 MB huge pages each small write copies a whole 2 MB page
fork() disables the page cache, so the snapshot file is held in anonymous memory
Redis switches to a slower allocator while a child process exists
os-memory-management:1.explanation: After fork, parent and child share pages read-only. Each page the parent modifies while the child is running gets copied. With THP the copy granularity is 2 MB instead of 4 KB, which magnifies the spike (Redis recommends disabling THP). The child does not copy the dataset up front; sharing is the whole point of fork.

os-memory-management:1.prompt: Where is a process's page table normally kept on a modern system, and how does the CPU find it?
options: In dedicated CPU registers, reloaded in full on every context switch
Inside the TLB, which holds the complete table
On disk, read in on every memory access
In main memory, located through a page-table base register (e.g., CR3 on x86)
os-memory-management:1.explanation: Page tables are far too large for registers, so they live in RAM and a base register points at the top level; a context switch just changes that register. The TLB caches a small number of recent translations, not the whole table.

os-memory-management:1.prompt: Which statements about paging are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A process's pages can be scattered across non-contiguous physical frames
Page sizes are powers of two so the address splits cleanly into page number and offset
Each process normally has its own page table
Paging eliminates internal fragmentation
The offset bits are translated through the page table along with the page number
os-memory-management:1.explanation: Pages map to any free frames, power-of-two sizes make the split a simple bit slice, and each address space has its own table. Internal fragmentation remains in the last page, and the offset is copied unchanged; only the page number is translated.

os-memory-management:1.prompt: Which fields does a conventional (non-inverted) page table entry typically contain? Select all that apply.
options: Physical frame number
Present/valid bit
Protection bits such as writable or user-accessible
The virtual page number it describes
The name of the file the page came from
os-memory-management:1.explanation: A PTE holds the frame number plus status and permission bits (present, dirty, accessed, R/W, user/supervisor, NX). The virtual page number is the index into the table, so it is not stored; file backing is tracked by kernel structures (e.g., VMAs), not by the PTE.

os-memory-management:1.prompt: Two processes can have page table entries pointing to the same physical frame, for example the read-only code pages of a shared library.
options: True
False
os-memory-management:1.explanation: True. Shared pages are a key benefit of paging: shared libraries, shared memory segments and copy-on-write pages after fork are all several PTEs referring to one frame.

os-memory-management:1.prompt: Doubling the page size halves the number of page table entries and also reduces internal fragmentation.
options: True
False
os-memory-management:1.explanation: False. Larger pages mean fewer entries, but the average waste in the last page grows (about half a page per region), so internal fragmentation increases. Page size is a trade-off between table size/TLB reach and fragmentation.

os-memory-management:2.prompt: In a pure segmentation scheme, what does a logical address consist of?
options: A page number and an offset
A segment number and an offset within that segment
A frame number and a limit
A single flat 32-bit number
os-memory-management:2.explanation: Segmentation exposes a two-part address <segment, offset>; the segment table supplies base and limit for each segment. <page, offset> is paging, where pages are fixed size and invisible to the programmer.

os-memory-management:2.prompt: Which kind of fragmentation is the main problem with pure segmentation?
options: Internal fragmentation within fixed-size pages
Fragmentation of the TLB
External fragmentation from variable-sized segments
Fragmentation of the segment table itself
os-memory-management:2.explanation: Segments have variable sizes, so allocating and freeing them leaves holes of assorted sizes in physical memory (external fragmentation), requiring compaction or best-fit strategies. Internal fragmentation is the paging problem.

os-memory-management:2.prompt: Segment 3 has base 3200 and limit 1100. What physical address does logical address <3, 852> map to?
os-memory-management:2.explanation: 852 < 1100, so the access is legal and physical = base + offset = 3200 + 852 = 4052. 4300 is base + limit, the end of the segment, not this byte.

os-memory-management:2.prompt: Segment 0 has base 1400 and limit 1000. A process references <0, 1222>. What happens?
options: Physical address 2622 is accessed
The hardware traps to the OS because the offset exceeds the limit
The access spills over into segment 1
Physical address 1222 is accessed
os-memory-management:2.explanation: The offset must be less than the limit (1000). 1222 fails the check, so the hardware traps (addressing error) before forming 2622. Silently spilling into another segment is exactly what limit checking prevents.

os-memory-management:2.prompt: Why is segmentation said to match the programmer's view of memory better than paging?
options: Segments correspond to logical units such as code, stack and heap, each with its own size and protection
Segments are always 4 KB, which matches typical function sizes
Segmentation needs no hardware support at all
Segments are invisible to the compiler, so programmers never think about them
os-memory-management:2.explanation: A program is naturally a set of variable-sized units (code, globals, heap, stack). Segmentation gives each a segment with its own limit and permissions, e.g., code read/execute and stack read/write. Fixed 4 KB units describe pages, not segments.

os-memory-management:2.prompt: Some architectures combine segmentation with paging (each segment is itself paged). What problem does this mainly solve?
options: It removes the need for a TLB
It lets segments exceed the size of the virtual address space
It removes external fragmentation, because segments no longer need contiguous physical memory
It eliminates internal fragmentation completely
os-memory-management:2.explanation: Paging each segment means a segment is a set of pages in any free frames, so variable-sized contiguous holes no longer matter. Internal fragmentation in the last page of each segment remains, and the TLB is still needed.

os-memory-management:2.prompt: In x86-64 long mode, segmentation is mostly disabled (CS/DS/ES/SS bases are treated as 0). What are the FS and GS segment registers still commonly used for?
options: Holding the page table base address
Thread-local storage and per-CPU data, via a non-zero base
Storing the return address of system calls
Enforcing stack limits for each thread
os-memory-management:2.explanation: FS and GS keep a usable base address, so OSes point them at per-thread data (e.g., TLS on Linux user space uses FS) or per-CPU kernel data (GS). The page table base is in CR3, not a segment register, and segment limits are not enforced in 64-bit mode.

os-memory-management:2.prompt: Two processes run the same editor. With segmentation, how can they share its code while keeping separate data?
options: Each process's segment table has an entry for the code segment pointing to the same base and limit, marked read-only/execute
The code is copied into each process's data segment at load time
Both processes share one segment table
Sharing is impossible with segmentation; it requires paging
os-memory-management:2.explanation: Sharing is natural in segmentation: both segment tables point at the same physical code segment with read/execute protection, while each has private data and stack segments. Sharing a whole segment table would share the data too.

os-memory-management:2.prompt: Which are advantages of segmentation? Select all that apply.
options: Protection can be set per logical unit, e.g., code read-only
A whole segment such as library code can be shared between processes
Segments like the stack can grow independently of one another
It avoids external fragmentation
Fixed-size units make physical allocation trivial
os-memory-management:2.explanation: Per-segment protection, sharing and independent growth are the selling points. Variable sizes cause external fragmentation, and fixed-size allocation describes paging, not segmentation.

os-memory-management:2.prompt: In a segmented system, which accesses cause a trap? Select all that apply.
options: Offset greater than or equal to the segment's limit
Segment number beyond the length of the segment table
A write to a segment marked read-only
Offset 0 in a valid, readable segment
A read of a code segment shared with another process
os-memory-management:2.explanation: The hardware checks the segment number against the table length, the offset against the limit, and the access type against the protection bits. Offset 0 is always within a valid segment, and reading a shared segment with read permission is legal.

os-memory-management:2.prompt: On modern Linux x86-64, a 'segmentation fault' almost always means a hardware segment limit was exceeded.
options: True
False
os-memory-management:2.explanation: False. The name is historical. Today SIGSEGV almost always comes from paging: touching an unmapped address (e.g., a null pointer) or violating page permissions such as writing to read-only memory. 64-bit mode does not even enforce segment limits.

os-memory-management:3.prompt: Under demand paging, what does the kernel do when a process touches a valid page that is not currently in memory?
options: Returns a zero to the process and continues
Restarts the whole process from the beginning
Brings the page into a free frame, updates the page table and restarts the faulting instruction
Moves the process to the back of the ready queue without loading anything
os-memory-management:3.explanation: The page fault handler finds a frame (evicting if needed), reads the page from disk (or zero-fills it), marks the PTE present and restarts the instruction so the process never notices. Only the instruction is restarted, not the whole process.

os-memory-management:3.prompt: What is the main benefit of demand paging compared with loading a whole program into memory at start-up?
options: Pages that are never used are never loaded, so start-up is faster and more processes fit in RAM
Page faults become impossible
It removes the need for swap or backing storage
Every memory access becomes faster
os-memory-management:3.explanation: Large parts of programs (error handlers, rarely used features) are never touched; demand paging skips loading them, saving I/O and memory. It adds page faults rather than removing them, and the pages still need backing storage.

os-memory-management:3.prompt: Memory access time is 200 ns and servicing a page fault takes 8 ms. If 1 in 1,000 accesses faults, what is the effective access time?
options: About 208 ns
About 8 ms
About 8.2 microseconds
About 2 microseconds
os-memory-management:3.explanation: EAT = 0.999 * 200 ns + 0.001 * 8,000,000 ns = 199.8 + 8,000 = about 8,200 ns (8.2 microseconds), roughly 40x slower than RAM. 208 ns comes from forgetting to convert 8 ms to 8,000,000 ns.

os-memory-management:3.prompt: With 200 ns memory access and 8 ms page fault service time, roughly what fault rate keeps the slowdown under 10% (effective access time below 220 ns)?
options: Fewer than 1 fault per 1,000 accesses
Fewer than 1 fault per 400,000 accesses
Fewer than 1 fault per 40 accesses
Fewer than 1 fault per 10 accesses
os-memory-management:3.explanation: 220 > 200 + p * 8,000,000 (approx.) gives p < 20 / 8,000,000 = 2.5e-6, i.e., under 1 fault per 400,000 accesses. Even 1 in 1,000 gives a ~40x slowdown, so demand paging only works because locality keeps fault rates tiny.

os-memory-management:3.prompt: A second instance of the same program starts while the first is running. It incurs many page faults but almost no disk reads. What kind of faults are these?
options: Major faults, each reading from swap
Segmentation faults that are silently ignored
Protection faults caused by copy-on-write
Minor faults: the pages are already in the page cache and only need to be mapped
os-memory-management:3.explanation: The executable and library pages are already cached in RAM from the first instance, so the fault handler only installs a mapping (a minor or soft fault). A major fault requires disk I/O, which is not happening here.

os-memory-management:3.prompt: On Linux with default overcommit settings, malloc(8 GB) succeeds on a 4 GB machine with no swap. Later the process gets killed while filling the buffer. Why?
options: malloc only reserved virtual address space; frames are allocated on first touch, and when RAM runs out the OOM killer picks a victim
malloc returned a pointer into kernel memory, which caused a protection fault
The kernel zeroes the whole 8 GB at malloc time and ran out of time
glibc rejects allocations over 4 GB at the first write
os-memory-management:3.explanation: Linux overcommits: the allocation creates virtual mappings with no frames behind them. Demand paging allocates frames as pages are touched; when memory is exhausted, the OOM killer terminates a process. Nothing is zeroed up front, which is why the malloc call itself was fast.

os-memory-management:3.prompt: A process touches a freshly allocated, never-used page of anonymous memory (e.g., new heap space). What does the page fault handler typically do?
options: Reads the page from the executable file on disk
Reads the page from swap
Maps a zero-filled frame without any disk read
Terminates the process for using uninitialized memory
os-memory-management:3.explanation: Anonymous memory has no file content, so the kernel provides a zeroed frame on first touch (zero-fill-on-demand). This is also a security measure so data from other processes never leaks. Swap is only read for pages that were previously swapped out.

os-memory-management:3.prompt: Which steps are part of handling a page fault on a valid page that is not resident? Select all that apply.
options: Trap into the kernel and check that the address is valid
Find a free frame, evicting a victim page if necessary
Schedule a disk read for the page and let another process run meanwhile
Mark the PTE present and restart the faulting instruction
Send SIGSEGV to the process
os-memory-management:3.explanation: The handler validates the address, gets a frame, does the I/O (the CPU runs something else while waiting), updates the page table and restarts the instruction. SIGSEGV is only for invalid accesses, not valid-but-absent pages.

os-memory-management:3.prompt: For which page faults does the kernel NOT need to read the page from disk? Select all that apply.
options: First touch of anonymous heap memory
A shared library page that another process already loaded into the page cache
A heap page that was previously written out to swap
The first access to a code page of a binary no process has run since boot
os-memory-management:3.explanation: Fresh anonymous memory is zero-filled and already-cached file pages just need mapping; both are minor faults. A swapped-out page must be read back from swap, and a cold binary's code must be read from the file system: both are major faults.

os-memory-management:3.prompt: Under pure demand paging, a process can start executing with none of its pages in memory.
options: True
False
os-memory-management:3.explanation: True. The very first instruction fetch faults, and every page is brought in only when first referenced. In practice OSes also prefetch (e.g., readahead) to reduce the initial burst of faults.

os-memory-management:3.prompt: With demand paging, a process's virtual address space cannot be larger than physical RAM.
options: True
False
os-memory-management:3.explanation: False. Only the pages in use need frames; the rest stay on disk or are never allocated. That is why a 64-bit process can map files or reserve address ranges far larger than RAM.

os-memory-management:4.prompt: Why can't the Optimal (OPT/MIN) page replacement algorithm be used in a real OS?
options: It needs too much memory for counters
It requires knowing which page will be referenced farthest in the future
It suffers from Belady's anomaly
It only works with a single frame
os-memory-management:4.explanation: OPT evicts the page whose next use is farthest away, which requires knowledge of future references. It is a stack algorithm, so it does not suffer Belady's anomaly; it is used offline as a benchmark.

os-memory-management:4.prompt: Which algorithm can exhibit Belady's anomaly, where adding frames increases the number of page faults?
options: LRU
Optimal (OPT)
FIFO
Least recently used with exact timestamps
os-memory-management:4.explanation: FIFO is not a stack algorithm: the set of pages in memory with n frames is not always a subset of the set with n+1 frames, so more frames can mean more faults. LRU and OPT are stack algorithms and never get worse with more frames.

os-memory-management:4.prompt: Reference string: 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. How many page faults does FIFO produce with 3 frames and with 4 frames?
options: 9 with 3 frames, 10 with 4 frames
10 with 3 frames, 9 with 4 frames
9 with 3 frames, 8 with 4 frames
12 with 3 frames, 6 with 4 frames
os-memory-management:4.explanation: This is the classic Belady's anomaly string: FIFO gives 9 faults with 3 frames but 10 with 4 frames. Assuming more frames must mean fewer faults (10 then 9) is exactly the intuition the anomaly breaks.

os-memory-management:4.prompt: For the reference string 7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4,2,3,0,3,2,1,2,0,1,7,0,1 with 3 frames, LRU causes how many page faults? (FIFO causes 15 and OPT causes 9.)
os-memory-management:4.explanation: Working through LRU (evicting the page unused for longest) gives 12 faults, between OPT's 9 and FIFO's 15. This textbook example shows LRU approximating OPT by using the recent past as a predictor of the near future.

os-memory-management:4.prompt: Clock (second-chance) replacement: frames hold A (ref bit 1), B (ref bit 0), C (ref bit 1), and the hand points at A. A fault occurs. What happens?
options: A is evicted because the hand points at it
A's bit is cleared, the hand moves on, and B is evicted
C is evicted because it was loaded most recently
All bits are cleared and A is evicted
os-memory-management:4.explanation: A page with ref bit 1 gets a second chance: its bit is cleared and the hand advances. B has bit 0, so it is evicted. Evicting whatever the hand points at regardless of the bit is plain FIFO.

os-memory-management:4.prompt: Enhanced second-chance uses (reference bit, dirty bit) pairs. Which class does it prefer to evict first?
options: (0, 1): not recently used but dirty
(1, 0): recently used but clean
(0, 0): not recently used and clean
(1, 1): recently used and dirty
os-memory-management:4.explanation: (0, 0) pages are unlikely to be needed soon and can be dropped without a write-back, so they are the cheapest victims. (0, 1) is next: not recently used, but eviction costs a disk write.

os-memory-management:4.prompt: Why do operating systems approximate LRU (e.g., with Clock or aging) rather than implementing it exactly?
options: Exact LRU needs to update a timestamp or reorder a list on every memory reference, which is far too expensive without special hardware
Exact LRU suffers from Belady's anomaly
Exact LRU needs knowledge of future references
Exact LRU only works for read-only pages
os-memory-management:4.explanation: Memory references happen billions of times per second; maintaining exact recency order on each would cost more than it saves. Hardware only sets a reference bit, which Clock and aging use cheaply. LRU does not need future knowledge (that is OPT) and has no Belady's anomaly.

os-memory-management:4.prompt: A nightly job sequentially reads a 200 GB file through an LRU-managed cache of 32 GB. Afterwards, hit rates for the daytime hot data collapse. What is going on, and what is the usual fix?
options: The file's pages are dirty and block eviction; the fix is to call fsync more often
LRU is evicting the scanned pages too early; the fix is a bigger LRU list
The cache has thrashed its page table; the fix is huge pages
Each scanned page becomes most-recently-used and pushes out the hot set; scan-resistant policies (2Q, ARC, LRU-K, or ring buffers for scans) fix it
os-memory-management:4.explanation: Pure LRU treats a once-only scan as recent use, so a large scan flushes the whole working set. Scan-resistant designs require a second access before promotion or isolate scans (PostgreSQL uses small ring buffers for big sequential scans). A bigger cache cannot hold a scan larger than itself.

os-memory-management:4.prompt: Which page replacement algorithms are immune to Belady's anomaly? Select all that apply.
options: LRU
Optimal (OPT)
FIFO
Any algorithm, as long as frames are only ever added
os-memory-management:4.explanation: LRU and OPT are stack algorithms: the pages held with n frames are always a subset of those held with n+1, so faults never increase. FIFO is not, and adding frames does not save an algorithm that lacks the stack property.

os-memory-management:4.prompt: Which mechanisms do real kernels use to approximate LRU recency cheaply? Select all that apply.
options: A hardware-set reference (accessed) bit in each PTE
Aging: periodically shifting reference bits into a per-page counter
A clock hand that sweeps frames and clears reference bits
Recording a precise timestamp in software on every memory load
Using only the dirty bit to decide which pages are hot
os-memory-management:4.explanation: Reference bits, aging counters and clock sweeps give an approximate recency signal at low cost. Per-access software timestamps are impossible at memory speed, and the dirty bit records writes, not recency, so it cannot tell hot read-only pages from cold ones.

os-memory-management:4.prompt: Although OPT cannot be implemented online, it is useful as a yardstick for measuring how close a practical algorithm comes to the best possible fault count.
options: True
False
os-memory-management:4.explanation: True. Given a recorded reference trace, OPT can be computed offline and gives the lower bound on faults, so researchers compare LRU, Clock, ARC and others against it.

options: A process using 100% CPU in a tight loop
Two threads repeatedly contending for the same lock
A disk failing and remapping sectors
The system spending more time servicing page faults than doing useful work
os-memory-management:5.explanation: Thrashing happens when processes do not have enough frames for their working sets: each fault evicts a page that is needed again soon, so the CPU mostly waits on paging I/O. Lock contention is a different problem.

os-memory-management:5.prompt: A naive scheduler sees CPU utilization falling and admits more processes to raise it. Why does this make thrashing worse?
options: New processes take frames from existing ones, raising the fault rate further and lowering CPU utilization even more
The scheduler's own code uses too much CPU
More processes increase the TLB size requirement beyond the hardware limit
The new processes are given lower priority and never run
os-memory-management:5.explanation: Low CPU utilization here comes from processes waiting on paging, not from a lack of work. More processes mean fewer frames each, so faults increase in a feedback loop. The fix is to reduce the degree of multiprogramming, not raise it.

os-memory-management:5.prompt: With a working-set window of 5 references, the most recent references are 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 3, 2, 4 (newest last). What is the working-set size now?
os-memory-management:5.explanation: The last 5 references are 4, 3, 3, 2, 4, whose distinct pages are {2, 3, 4}, so the size is 3. Counting all distinct pages ever referenced (4) ignores the window.

os-memory-management:5.prompt: Using the working-set model, the sum of all processes' working-set sizes exceeds the number of available frames. What should the OS do?
options: Increase the working-set window so that more pages fit
Suspend (swap out) one or more processes and give their frames to the others
Admit more processes to raise CPU utilization
Switch from LRU to FIFO replacement
os-memory-management:5.explanation: If total demand D exceeds available frames, someone will thrash; suspending a process frees frames so the rest can hold their working sets. Increasing the window makes demand larger, not smaller.

os-memory-management:5.prompt: In page-fault-frequency (PFF) control, a process's fault rate rises above the upper threshold. What does the OS do?
options: Takes frames away from the process
Terminates the process
Allocates more frames to the process, or suspends a process if none are free
Lowers the process's CPU priority
os-memory-management:5.explanation: A high fault rate means the process has too few frames, so it gets more; below the lower threshold it has more than it needs and loses some. If no frames are free, a process is suspended. Taking frames away would push it further into thrashing.

os-memory-management:5.prompt: Why is global page replacement more prone to spreading thrashing than local replacement?
options: Global replacement cannot use reference bits
A process short of frames can steal frames from other processes, pushing them into thrashing too
Global replacement forces all processes to use the same page size
Local replacement lets a process take frames from the kernel
os-memory-management:5.explanation: With global replacement, a thrashing process evicts other processes' pages, which raises their fault rates too. Local replacement confines a process to its own frames, so its thrashing hurts mostly itself (though it still slows the shared paging device).

os-memory-management:5.prompt: A Java or Node.js service with a large heap starts swapping on a memory-tight host, and latency becomes terrible during garbage collection. Why are garbage-collected runtimes especially hurt by swap?
options: GC disables the page cache while running
Swapped pages are always compressed, so GC must decompress them
The kernel refuses to swap heap pages, so GC fails
A collection traverses many live objects across the heap, faulting in swapped-out pages one after another
os-memory-management:5.explanation: Marking and compacting touch large parts of the heap, effectively defeating locality: every swapped-out page the collector reaches is a major fault. That turns a pause of milliseconds into seconds, which is why such services usually run with swap avoided and memory limits sized to the working set.

os-memory-management:5.prompt: Which observations on a Linux host point to thrashing? Select all that apply.
options: High swap-in and swap-out rates (si/so in vmstat)
A very high rate of major page faults
Low user CPU time with high I/O wait
High user CPU time with almost no disk activity
A large 'buff/cache' value in free with plenty of 'available' memory
os-memory-management:5.explanation: Thrashing shows as heavy swap traffic, many major faults and CPUs idle waiting on I/O. High user CPU with no disk I/O is compute-bound work, and a large page cache with plenty of available memory is a healthy system.

os-memory-management:5.prompt: Which actions reduce or prevent thrashing? Select all that apply.
options: Reducing the degree of multiprogramming
Adding physical memory
Improving locality in the program's access patterns
Starting more processes to keep the CPU busy
Switching to more aggressive global replacement
os-memory-management:5.explanation: Fewer competing processes, more RAM or smaller working sets (better locality) all let each process keep its working set resident. More processes and more aggressive stealing between them make the shortage worse.

os-memory-management:5.prompt: In the working-set model, a window that is too small fails to capture the whole locality, and one that is too large spans several localities.
options: True
False
os-memory-management:5.explanation: True. Too small a window under-estimates the pages needed (causing faults); too large over-estimates them (wasting frames and reducing multiprogramming). Choosing the window is the model's key tuning problem.

os-memory-management:5.prompt: When thrashing causes low CPU utilization, scheduling more processes will bring utilization back up.
options: True
False
os-memory-management:5.explanation: False. Utilization is low because processes are blocked on paging. Adding processes shrinks everyone's frame allocation and increases faults further; the remedy is fewer processes or more memory.

os-memory-management:6.prompt: What does the translation lookaside buffer (TLB) cache?
options: Recently used data bytes from main memory
Recently used virtual-to-physical page translations
Pages recently written to swap
File blocks recently read from disk
os-memory-management:6.explanation: The TLB is a small, fast cache of page table entries, so most translations avoid walking the page table in memory. Data bytes live in the L1/L2/L3 caches and file blocks in the OS page cache.

os-memory-management:6.prompt: Memory access takes 100 ns and TLB lookup time is negligible. With an 80% TLB hit ratio and a single-level page table, what is the effective memory access time?
options: 100 ns
180 ns
200 ns
120 ns
os-memory-management:6.explanation: Hit: 100 ns (one access). Miss: 200 ns (page table access + data access). EAT = 0.8 * 100 + 0.2 * 200 = 80 + 40 = 120 ns. 180 ns comes from swapping the hit and miss weights.

os-memory-management:6.prompt: x86-64 4-level paging splits a 48-bit virtual address into four 9-bit indexes plus a 12-bit offset. Why 9 bits per level?
options: A 4 KB page-table page holds 512 eight-byte entries, and 512 = 2^9
There are 9 general-purpose registers for page walking
48 divided by 5 rounds to 9
Each level must cover exactly 9 GB
os-memory-management:6.explanation: Each page table level occupies exactly one 4 KB page; 4096 / 8 = 512 entries, which needs 9 index bits. 4 * 9 + 12 = 48, matching the virtual address width.

os-memory-management:6.prompt: A 64-entry data TLB maps 4 KB pages. If the application switches to 2 MB huge pages, how does the TLB reach (memory covered without misses) change?
options: From 64 KB to 64 MB
It stays at 256 KB; page size does not affect reach
From 256 KB to 128 MB
From 4 MB to 2 GB
os-memory-management:6.explanation: Reach = entries * page size: 64 * 4 KB = 256 KB, and 64 * 2 MB = 128 MB, a 512x increase. That is why databases and JVMs with large heaps often benefit from huge pages.

os-memory-management:6.prompt: How do ASIDs (or PCIDs on x86) improve performance on context switches?
options: They let TLB entries be tagged per address space, so the TLB need not be flushed on every switch
They double the number of TLB entries
They make page faults impossible after a switch
They let the kernel skip saving registers
os-memory-management:6.explanation: Without tags, entries from the old process would be wrong for the new one, so the TLB must be flushed and refilled with misses. Tagging entries with an address-space ID lets entries from several processes coexist. The number of entries is unchanged.

os-memory-management:6.prompt: Why does a multi-level page table use much less memory than a flat table for a typical process?
options: It stores entries compressed
It uses larger pages automatically
It keeps page table entries on disk
Inner tables are only allocated for regions of the address space actually in use, which is sparse
os-memory-management:6.explanation: A process uses a few regions (code, heap, stacks, mappings) in a huge address space. Unused regions just have an empty entry at an upper level and no lower-level tables at all. The cost is extra memory references per TLB miss.

os-memory-management:6.prompt: A heavily multithreaded process on a 64-core server frequently calls munmap and mprotect, and those calls scale poorly as threads increase. What is the most likely reason?
options: munmap must zero every unmapped page synchronously
Each mapping change requires a TLB shootdown: interrupting every CPU that may cache the old translation so it invalidates it
The page table becomes read-only while threads are running
The kernel serializes all system calls from one process
os-memory-management:6.explanation: TLBs are per CPU and not coherent with page table writes, so after changing or removing a mapping the kernel sends inter-processor interrupts to other CPUs running the process and waits for them to invalidate. More cores and threads mean more expensive shootdowns. Zeroing pages happens on allocation, not unmapping.

os-memory-management:6.prompt: Which events require invalidating TLB entries? Select all that apply.
options: Changing a PTE from writable to read-only, as when marking pages copy-on-write after fork
Unmapping a page
Switching address spaces on a CPU without ASID/PCID support
A read from a page that is already mapped
A TLB hit on a valid entry
os-memory-management:6.explanation: Any change that makes a cached translation stale (permission downgrade, unmapping, new address space without tags) needs invalidation. Ordinary reads and TLB hits change nothing in the page tables, so no invalidation is needed.

os-memory-management:6.prompt: Which of these reduce TLB misses or their cost? Select all that apply.
options: Using huge pages for large, hot memory regions
Improving spatial locality of data accesses
Tagging TLB entries with ASIDs/PCIDs
Adding more page table levels
Using smaller pages
os-memory-management:6.explanation: Huge pages increase reach, better locality touches fewer pages, and tagged entries survive context switches. Extra levels make each miss more expensive, and smaller pages reduce reach so misses increase.

os-memory-management:6.prompt: Multi-level page tables save memory but make each TLB miss more expensive, because the page walk needs one memory reference per level.
options: True
False
os-memory-management:6.explanation: True. A 4-level walk needs up to four memory references before the data access. Hardware mitigates this with page-walk caches and data caches, but the trade-off is real and is why TLB hit rates matter so much.

os-memory-management:6.prompt: Every TLB miss causes a page fault that the operating system must handle.
options: True
False
os-memory-management:6.explanation: False. On x86 a TLB miss triggers a hardware page walk; if the PTE is present, the TLB is refilled with no OS involvement. A page fault happens only if the walk finds the page not present or the access not permitted.
